report.source_text: Physical exam was significant for swelling over the neck and shoulders with underlying palpable crepitus, lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally with equal chest wall excursion, regular heart rate and rhythm, head atraumatic and normocephalic, neck atraumatic, edematous oropharynx extending to the posterior pharynx, and lip and tongue swelling. The patient had a muffled voice noted with tonsillar pillars touching during phonation and did not have any rashes or neurologic deficits.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 19-year-old male presented to the ED after diving without equipment, experiencing voice change, face/neck swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Physical exam revealed swelling and palpable crepitus over the neck and shoulders, an edematous oropharynx, and a muffled voice. Due to progressive symptoms and concern for airway compromise, he was intubated. CT imaging showed diffuse interstitial emphysema throughout both lungs, suggesting mediastinal and subcutaneous emphysema, and extensive emphysema of the neck. He was admitted to the ICU for pulmonary barotrauma, successfully extubated the next day, and his subcutaneous emphysema improved. He was advised to avoid diving and to undergo outpatient pulmonary evaluation.

Physical examination revealed signs of air leak, including swelling and palpable crepitus over the neck and shoulders, edematous oropharynx, and muffled voice.
CT chest revealed diffuse interstitial emphysema throughout both lungs, suggesting mediastinal and subcutaneous emphysema, consistent with pulmonary barotrauma.
CT neck showed extensive emphysema of the neck.
Patient required intubation due to progressive presentation and concern for airway compromise, and was admitted to the ICU for pulmonary barotrauma.
Clinical course included successful extubation and improving subcutaneous emphysema, with recommendations for follow-up and avoidance of diving.
